lines.text: I see I cannot get thy father’s love;
Therefore no more turn me to him, sweet Nan.
Alas! how then?
Why, thou must be thyself.
He doth object, I am too great of birth;
And that my state being gall’d with my expense,
I seek to heal it only by his wealth.
Besides these, other bars he lays before me,
My riots past, my wild societies;
And tells me ’tis a thing impossible
I should love thee but as a property.
May be he tells you true.
No, heaven so speed me in my time to come!
Albeit I will confess thy father’s wealth
Was the first motive that I wooed thee, Anne:
Yet, wooing thee, I found thee of more value
Than stamps in gold, or sums in sealèd bags;
And ’tis the very riches of thyself
That now I aim at.
Gentle Master Fenton,
Yet seek my father’s love; still seek it, sir.
If opportunity and humblest suit
Cannot attain it, why then⁠—hark you hither.

blocks.text: Enter Justice Shallow, Slender, and Mistress Quickly.
Break their talk, Mistress Quickly: my kinsman shall speak for himself. She draws near the lovers.

lines.text: Pale. I’ll make a shaft or a bolt on’t. ’Slid, ’tis but venturing.
Be not dismayed.
No, she shall not dismay me. I care not for that, but that I am afeard.
To Anne Page. Hark ye; Master Slender would speak a word with you.
I come to him. Aside.
This is my father’s choice.
O, what a world of vile ill-favour’d faults
Looks handsome in three hundred pounds a year!

blocks.text: Steps between them. And how does good Master Fenton? Pray you, a word with you. Anne moves away.

lines.text: She’s coming; to her, coz. O boy, thou hadst a father!

blocks.text: I had a father, Mistress Anne; my uncle can tell you good jests of him. Pray you, uncle, tell Mistress Anne the jest how my father stole two geese out of a pen, good uncle.

lines.text: Mistress Anne, my cousin loves you.
Ay, that I do; as well as I love any woman in Gloucestershire.
He will maintain you like a gentlewoman.
Ay, that I will come cut and long-tail, under the degree of a squire.
He will make you a hundred and fifty pounds jointure.
Good Master Shallow, let him woo for himself.

blocks.text: Marry, I thank you for it; I thank you for that good comfort. She calls you, coz; I’ll leave you. He stands aside.

lines.text: Now, Master Slender.
Plucking his beard. Now, good Mistress Anne.⁠—
What is your will?

blocks.text: My will! ’od’s heartlings, that’s a pretty jest indeed! I ne’er made my will yet, I thank heaven; I am not such a sickly creature, I give heaven praise.

lines.text: I mean, Master Slender, what would you with me?

blocks.text: Casting down his eyes. Truly, for mine own part I would little or nothing with you. Your father and my uncle hath made motions; if it be my luck, so; if not, happy man be his dole! They can tell you how things go better than I can. You may ask your father; here he comes.

lines.text: Now, Master Slender: love him, daughter Anne.
Why, how now! what does Master Fenton here?
You wrong me, sir, thus still to haunt my house:
I told you, sir, my daughter is dispos’d of.
Nay, Master Page, be not impatient.
Good Master Fenton, come not to my child.
She is no match for you.
Sir, will you hear me?
No, good Master Fenton.
Come, Master Shallow; come, son Slender, in.
Knowing my mind, you wrong me, Master Fenton.

blocks.text: Exeunt Page, Justice Shallow, and Slender.

lines.text: Speak to Mistress Page.
Good Mistress Page, for that I love your daughter
In such a righteous fashion as I do,
Perforce, against all checks, rebukes, and manners,
I must advance the colours of my love
And not retire: let me have your good will.
Good mother, do not marry me to yond fool.
I mean it not; I seek you a better husband.
That’s my master, Master doctor.
Alas! I had rather be set quick i’ the earth.
And bowl’d to death with turnips.
Come, trouble not yourself. Good Master Fenton,
I will not be your friend, nor enemy;
My daughter will I question how she loves you,
And as I find her, so am I affected.
Till then, farewell, sir: she must needs go in;
Her father will be angry.

blocks.text: Exeunt Mistress Page. Anne Page follows, turning at the door.

lines.text: Farewell, gentle mistress. Farewell, Nan.

blocks.text: This is my doing now: “Nay,” said I, “will you cast away your child on a fool, and a physician? Look on Master Fenton.” This is my doing.

lines.text: I thank thee; and I pray thee, once tonight
Give my sweet Nan this ring. There’s for thy pains.

blocks.text: Fenton thrusts money in her hands and exits.

Now Heaven send thee good fortune! A kind heart he hath; a woman would run through fire and water for such a kind heart. But yet I would my master had Mistress Anne; or I would Master Slender had her; or, in sooth, I would Master Fenton had her; I will do what I can for them all three, for so I have promised, and I’ll be as good as my word; but speciously for Master Fenton. Well, I must of another errand to Sir John Falstaff from my two mistresses: what a beast am I to slack it!
